Hello Everyone,

I have a question for the forum. I just shot another Yugioh hologram last night, a 5 layer 2d-3d full color one. Pretty standard for what I do. 

Here's the question. I used only one laser to do these, transmission rainbows, but made them from color separations. Would you consider this real color or pseudo color?

Is it pseudo color because I used only one laser?

Is it real color because I used proper separations and not hand painting a model or something else that's subjective? Even with one laser those separations carry the real color info that has been recorded faithfully on the H1. That color can later be recreated at the right angle with a rainbow H2. 

Is it pseudo color just because it's a rainbow and needs to be tilted to the right angle to get the colors correct?

Does it switch between pseudo and real color as it's brought into the correct viewing angle?

Is it pseudo color because I didn't set my angles that determine the color exactly to a correct set of 3 frequencies? If I had, would it then be real color?

What are your thoughts?

 Jeffrey Weil

 NorthBeach Holography Inc.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
Jeez, Jeff! Talk about cat amongst the pigeons! Asking "what is pseudo-colour?" is a bit like whether McDonalds tastes better than Burger King! The whole question is mostly subjective, one person's "pseudo-colour" is another person's "true colour", especially in these rainbow holograms.

Here's my take, for what it's worth. Let's start with what colour is. Colour is a sensation on the eye, interpreted by the brain, of the natural world. You may remember that essay I did on colour perception (which is apparently all over the web - I'm surprised that non-holographers would be interested in that at all!). Anyway, continuing, the real world produces colour by means of natural pigments created out of proteins, atomic structure etc. In this sense, colours in the real world cannot be "wrong". If you see real blue grass, then the colour of the grass is not "wrong" because grass is supposed to be green, this is just a variant of grass.

 However, when it comes to reproducing colour in some medium, then the job of the reconstruction process is to produce a colour that is recognisable by association to the real world. So, if you print a picture with pink grass, then we all "know" that grass is "really" green and the pink grass is "art". The observer of the picture cannot know whether the photographer really found pink grass in nature. But, there a gazillion real colours in nature, so we use a reduction process which takes advantage of the fact that we have only three colour receptors in our eyes - red, green and blue (the exact wavelengths of these receptors in the eye is in that essay I mentioned). We use three basic primaries and reproduce all the colours of nature with these primaries in various proportions - out-of-gamut and negative-coefficient colour notwithstanding for now. However, we choose the proportions to give us a deliberate copy of nature - green for grass - or an exaggerated unnatural effect - pink for grass. We can pretty much make any object any colour by simply changing the proportions of the primaries. We can even alter the inputs from electronic equipment to alter real-world colours to bizarre unnatural colours by simply changing the white point in the camera. 

In holography, the colours of a hologram are generated by fringe separation or by diffraction angles, or both. In fact, you could argue that both these methods are actually the same method. So, colour is not an intrinsic property of the medium, as it is in print media or film, but a by-product of a physical process. You can control this physical process in a number of ways:

1. Swell the emulsion

2. Change the angles of the reference

3. Expose the film with different wavelengths.

All of these methods alter the physical process of the playback and generate "colours". But, do they generate "real" colours, ie do they generate the actual colours of a real-world object or scene. 

You could argue that the reproduction of "real" colours are those that are captured directly from a real world object or scene by some capture method (camera etc) and reproduced in a medium (eg film) with no alteration of or by the medium *and* by the capturing method. So, a photo of grass focused onto colour film by a camera is "real" colour" when there are no filters on the camera and the colour on the film is a faithful reproduction of the colour of the grass, albeit artificially reproduced by dyes in the film. 

If the colour of a real world object or scene is altered by some physical device (eg filters) or by some processing scheme on the media (eg non-standard development), then the "colour" is not a real world colour captured faithfully, but imposed onto the medium by a physical or procedural process. In this case, you could call the the resulting colour "pseudo-colour" - 'pseudo' because it's not the actual colour of the real object, but a false colour imposed by your process. 

In holography, a faithful reproduction of colour would imply that the process whereby a hologram is both recorded and reconstructed would capture colour information faithfully and reconstruct it faithfully. But, holography is a diffractive process. What comes out of a hologram is not "colour", but a reconstituted set of pure wavelengths given by the fringe separation. Our eyes do not see pure wavelengths because the receptors in our eyes are not pure red, green and blue; there's a massive superimposition of the wavelength peaks (again the exact wavelength sensitivity of the retinal dyes are in that essay). So, whatever fringes are recorded in the hologram, they must diffract the exact same wavelength combinations that are recognised by the eye brain system as "true colour". In holography also, the colour of the source is very impportant; if the colour in the source does not contain the colour in the hologram, it ain't going to diffract. So now the reconstruction process involves not only the medium, but the reconstruction of that medium.

So, pseudo colour in holography is generally considered to be swelling the emulsion - an artificial manipulation of the colour reproduction system by artificially altering the fringe separation. In your case of rainbows, that too would be pseudocolour because you're artificially generating a specific colour(s) by manipulation of the reference beams - you decide which reference beam angle you want to impose a particular colour rather than let nature and an unaltered capture system decide on the colour. You can make grass pink if you chose to, by simply altering the reference angle. However, I could argue that *all colour holography* is pseudo-colour because even "true colour" holography with three (or more) lasers is still manipulation of the medium to get the "right colours" - in this case getting the chemistry right.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **kaveh1000:** If one laser, then it is pseudocolor, because you are choosing where to put the colors

Can't you use two lasers and swell? For example, if I wanted a dark green with blue tonal variations, could I shoot with an Argon (514) and, say, a C315 (532) and then swell? By choosing the swell rate, I can create a deep green with with an overtone of light blue. I can do this without using a pan medium because both wavelengths are close enough that the same emulsion, VRP for example, can take both colours.

I don't think it's the number of lasers, I think it's the (artificial) manipulation of colours - the creation of "your own" colours - that makes the essence of pseudocolour. But, since the colours from a hologram are as much in the chemistry as in the recording, is the chemical manipulation of a hologram also pseudocolour? For instance, if I shoot a yellow object with a red and green laser, it's quite difficult to get a yellow hologram; the hologram has to be carefully processed. Is the care in the processing a pseudocolour technique or should you just let the hologram diffract whatever it wants to and call that the natural tendency of the medium - a faithful representation within the limits of the medium?

By the way, there is no right or wrong answer. As I said earlier, this is largely a matter of subjective interpretation and opinion. I do think it's an interesting discussion, though, since it goes to the heart of what "colour" means in a holographic sense. Incidentally, for what it's worth, Peter Miller calls Jeff's example " transmission pseudo-colour . That is, the superimposition of two or more slits to reconstruct at the same eye position is transmission pseudocolour . But, if you make a 5 H1 resist and have two of the elements in the same colour, is it still pseudocolour? It is according to Peter; two slits are superimposing on the same eye position - it's just that the slits are displaying the same colour.

posts.author: Gall
posts.content_md:
I personally like the following definitions:

"Pseudo color" in holography is the color that is not related to the reflection spectrum of the object and is created solely by special processing using single laser wavelength. Much like painted b&w photograph.

"Real color" is the color caused by different reflection of different wavelengths by the object. Here we have to distinguish between "just real color" (using 3 or sometimes 2 lasers) and "true color" that represents the full spectrum (like Lippmann photography). Looks like "true color" is impossible in holography.

posts.author: Gall
posts.content_md:
Hm... It's not about the resulting image, it's about the recording process.

Consider a red cardboard with one green strip and one black strip. Let's use a single He-Ne laser to record a pseudo-color hologram. Even if we do recording with different angles and/or with chemical pre- and postprocessing, we'll get two black strips on the hologram. We have to "paint" the green one by hand, i.e. masking them with a piece of white tape while recording the "green" color? that is, recording a different object instead! Using two lasers in a "real color" process, we'll able to record that strip without any modification to the object.

Consider another model. Take something refractive. Let's make a hologram of ambient light coming through a glass prism spectroscope. Then illuminate hologram with white light.

If the hologram shows the full spectrum of white light, call it "true color". (This seems to be impossible).

If the hologram shows narrow colorful lines on correct places for their wavelengths or shifted just a little bit, call it "real color".

If the hologram shows lines on incorrect places (i.e. a green line at "650 nm" mark), call it "pseudo color".

posts.author: PinkysBrain
posts.content_md:
> **Gall:** If the hologram shows lines on incorrect places (i.e. a green line at "650 nm" mark), call it "pseudo color".

If it's intended it's right where it should be, calling that incorrect is rather biased. Also with that kind of thinking you can still get two identical holograms and you will be forced to call one pseudo colour and the other real colour based on an artifact of the recording process. Pseudo colour should not be used as an adjective for the holograms themselves, it's just plain confusing. Pseudo colour holography, fine, pseudo colour recorded hologram, fine too ... pseudo colour hologram, not so much.

If a hologram is meant to replay with multiple colours in a single view but the colour components during replay are not the same as the wavelength(s) used for recording, call the recording method pseudo colour.

PS. this is of course assuming you want to extend the term pseudo colour beyond just the swelling method in the first place, some authors have done so already in published articles ... but you can always just decide to disagree with them.

Here we have to distinguish between "just real color" (using 3 or sometimes 2 lasers) and "true color" that represents the full spectrum (like Lippmann photography). ..with some reservations.I'm not sure how Gall differentiates between "just real colour" using two or three lasers and "true colour", presumably also using two or three lasers. If "true colour" means a faithful recording of a coloured object while "just real colour" means recording a coloured object and getting an unfaithful representation, then it seems to me that the difference lies in the technique (exposures, beam ratios, wavelength ratios) and the chemistry. If the above is true, then it is possible to get a fairly faithful representation of the colours in a coloured object (see below).

> **Gall:** Consider a red cardboard with one green strip and one black strip.

> **Gall:** Using two lasers in a "real color" process, we'll able to record that strip without any modification to the object.

But, if you record your box with one green stripe and one black stripe and the hologram shows one green and one black stripe, then isn't this also "true colour"? Is Gail saying that if I painted an entire spectrum on the box and then recorded it, only a subset of the stripes would show on the hologram, or that some colours would be faithfully recorded and some not so faithfully; and if the entire set showed on the hologram, then it'd be "true colour"? 

> **PinkysBrain:** Lets say you could record the exact same hologram with the exact same fringes with 3 exposures with 3 objects and exposure angles with one wavelength, and with 1 exposure with 1 object and three wavelengths. Would it make sense to call one pseudo colour and one real colour? Even though they are identical?

Doesn't this get to the heart of what is meant by "colour" in holography? It seems to me that the observer is left out of these discussions and the interaction of the observer and the creator seems to me to be the vital link. The technique whereby the colours end up on the finished piece is hidden from the observer, so it seems to me that 'pseudocolour' in holography is no different to a photographer using a set of filters to enhance the colour variations on a photograph. However, no photographer would call it "pseudo-colour photograph". Whoever invented the term (I thought it was Fred Unterseher, apologies to Jeff if I was wrong!) presumably did so historically because the colours in a scene could either be recorded with multiple lasers, or, if you didn't have multiple lasers, could be recorded with one laser. Historically, this way was an easy way to impose colours on the cheap and the artificial imposition of the colours were "pseudo" because the colours were recorded in some fake way - you didn't record the *actual* colours coming off the real object. However, the work of John Kaufman shows that the colours can be surreal and still be pseudocolour. Could those rocks be made into the colours that Kauffman made be done with three lasers. Yes. Simply colour the rocks first. I think that today terms like "pseudo-colour" have lost their meaning because you no longer need to artificially impose colours on a scene. In the end, it's up to the observer what the impact of the colours are - whatever technique was used in making them. Some of Dave Battin's work is pretty striking. I have no idea, at first glance, whether he uses swelling or multiple lasers. Personally, I don't care, I just appreciate the play of colours in the work.

In terms of the observer, let's say your three objects are a pink box, a yellow box and an orange box. If you recorded all three objects with three lasers and got a faithful image, that is: a hologram showing a pink box, an yellow box and an orange box. Now you show that hologram to a friend. Your friend will say, "That's a colour hologram". Now, still staying with the three lasers, let's say that the pink box shows red in the hologram, the yellow shows as blue and the orange shows as green. Then, your friend will say, "That's a colour hologram". If I shot each box individually with one laser, one shot at a time and swelled between each shot. Now I make my pink box swell to green, my yellow box swell to red and my orange box I leave alone. Your friend will still say, "That's a colour hologram" Your friend has no idea what the original scene looked like. So, to your friend (the observer) you've either made three colour holograms, a "true colour" hologram a la Gall, a "real colour hologram" - also a la Gall, or a pseudocolour hologram. Is the differentiation then only in the head of the holographer?

posts.author: Gall
posts.content_md:
Talking about the resulting image, one may have 3 situations. The difference in color between the original and the image can be:

1 - easily viewed with bare eye

2 - (almost) invisible for bare eye but can be found using spectral measurements

3 - is (almost) invisible even through a spectroscope.

If we consider the process, there are also 3 situations:

1 - each color of the resulting image is recorded from the reflection of light of similar wavelength from the object

2 - each color of the resulting image is recorded from the reflection of light of significantly different wavelength. Manual color correction methods are applied to achieve the correct color representation if it is correct at all.

3 - there is no object at all, it's a digital 3d model

CMYK reproduces the components our eyes need by isolating them from the white light that hits the printed page, hence the CMYK components are the inverse of the RGB components. As you know, to get red, you print its inverse, thus the white light hitting the printed page has all but red removed, leaving red. Again, if you do not illuminate a printed page, ie look at it in the dark, then you receive black. If you do not illuminate a hologram, you also receive black. Maybe that’s what you know, but anyone who really knows how RGB and CMYK are related, to get red, you print the inverses of green and blue, magenta and yellow, to absorb their complements, green and blue, thus leaving only the red component reflected from the white light. If you print the inverse of red, which is cyan, you get the other two of the color trinity reflected, which are green and blue.

> Isn't this reconstruction in CMYK? It seems that in holography the recording process is RGB, but the reconstruction process is CMYK.

It looks like you’re missing the basic principle of the two modes of color reproduction: either add up to white with R, G, & B light sources, or start with white and subtract down to black using layers of C, M, Y, and sometimes K. (Chemical color films and prints do not use black dyes; printing presses and inkjet printers do use it.)

Since the hologram can be construed as altering the replay light, it acts like a light source, and its mode of color reproduction uses the additive primaries of RGB, like a monitor. That might explain why your image above is so hard to see!

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **PinkysBrain:** Colour holograms tend to be RBG reconstructions, so it's more about white point than temperature.

The association of colour temperatures to a white point is common in digital photography to take account of ambient conditions. The white point is that point where the coordinates, x-bar, y-bar and g-bar for example, are equal, so a specific white point is defined with respect to a specific colour chart - CIE 1931, CIE 1976, CIELAB etc. However, an absolute colour temperature regardless of any specific colour chart can be assigned as the radiation emitted by a black body at a given temperature. In this case, the colour temperature would be follow Planck's Law, or Wien's Law, or the Rayleigh Jeans Law, depending on the range of temperatures over which the source emits. 

Whether or not a colour temperature can be assigned to a LED is problematical, since the LED does not emit Planckian radiation. The same is true of fluorescent light bulbs, but they've gotten around that by assigning a colour temperature to the fluorescent source as to a Planckian source giving off the same radiation

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
The so-called color temperature of fluorescent lights is a trick pulled by the manufacturers. A color temperature meter, like those used in photography, is not a broadband spectrometer. It is simply red and blue filters in front of two separate light meters. The ratio of the red to blue readings gives a color temperature by looking at two points on the black body radiation curve.

Take a look at a color temperature rated fluorescent tube through a grating, or bounced off a CD, and you will see that distinctive strong green line indicative of the mercury emission, which might be ignored by the above-mentioned device or lumped in with the red reading.

Just another reason to hate those bulbs!

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
My idea of a "true" or "real" color hologram is one made with two or more laser wavelengths, with the final image being fairly close in color to the appearance of the object under those same laser wavelengths. If someone is limited to only two wavelengths, then I would say it's necessary to choose and apply appropriate colors to the object, to get the necessary color control. Three lasers would make things a lot easier, because ordinary objects can look quite close to their natrual-light appearance by using 3 correctly-chosen wavelengths.

Of course it will never be absolutely "true" or "real" color, no matter how much technology is involved (at least, I can't imagine this). But to me, this doesn't matter. "Close" is quite good enough. In a similar way, there is no such thing as a "holo" gram, because it never absolutely re-creates the "whole" picture. 

Reconstruction is of course a problem with color holograms. In my opinion, the best approach is to use an integrated concept where each hologram has it's own built-in illumination system. I think LEDs are the way to go. It's easy to buy a batch of 50 to 500 LEDs at a reasonable cost, and limit your editon of holograms to 50 to 500 pieces.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **PinkysBrain:** Any way ... my point about white point was that the hologram itself does not emit a smooth spectrum. A light with R/G/B leds at appropriate wavelengths might have poor CRI, but as long as the white point was right it would be as good as any lamp with a continuous spectrum to replay a hologram.

Well, actually, a hologram does not emit anything. It diffracts light from a set of interference planes at specific frequencies with specific strengths which are proportional to both the efficiency of the medium and the Bragg plane strength; in other words, a pure phase hologram in, say, dcg with a particular index modulation will have an output intensity that's a particular fraction of the input intensity. The same phase hologram in silver will have a different output intensity for the same input intensity because the scattering profile from point scatterers of reduced grains is different from the scattering profile from a continuous medium. 

This may seem overly pedantic, but I mention this because the discussion so far has focused on some sort of objective measurement of the frequency as a metaphor for "colour". However, colour is not a set of wavelengths, it's a subjective impression. As such, we need to take into account the photopic curve over which we interpret colour. For example, if our equipment reads a "blue" at 457nm of m units (say, candelas), then how do we perceive that "blue" (we actually can't, since a single frequency cannot be seen) ? If we measure a band of frequencies from 457 to 488 and at b units, then again, how do we perceive this "colour"? What colour is a yellow brick, as opposed to what are the band of frequencies, and with what strengths, can such a yellow brick be measured? 

Also, in terms of colour, there is a statistical component that I don't think has been appreciated yet. Let's say, for example, that your "red" fringes fall off as a Gaussian centered at 633 (the frequency cannot be a Dirac spike simply because of differential swelling, which cannot be avoided). In this case, a flat white source - one that a constant intensity across the visible spectrum - will diffract a "red" intensity according to the sigma on the Gaussian. This diffracted "red" will then have to be convolved with the scotopic curve to determine what "red" the observer actually sees. If you use a led, then the spectrum of the led will have to be convolved with the Gaussian of the fringe frequencies (which will depend on the sigma of the response curve) and then convolved again with the scotopic. All of this is again true of the other sets of fringe frequencies.

Remember also, the cone response functions don't peak at specific wavelengths. There's a great deal of overlap, resulting in, for example, wavelengths surrounding 600nm giving a large "green" response at the cones. 

> **BobH:** My guess is that the CRI of all reflection holography would be pretty low.

My guess is that the colur rendition is pretty low because the Gaussians of the three frequency components overlap. If you look at the cone responses, a large spread (large value of sigma) in the "red" components will give more of a green response and make the red appear yellowish.

> **Joe Farina:** Of course it will never be absolutely "true" or "real" color, no matter how much technology is involved (at least, I can't imagine this).

Why not? Is TV "real" or "true" colour. No colour reproduction is ever "real" because we have no idea what the original colour was. We have a mental picture of what's being portrayed and let our imaginations (or memories) do the rest. If you see a field of green grass, for example, you'd think that it's "true" colour because that's what the colour of grass is. But if you take you "colour-meter" and measure real grass and then take that same meter and measure the picture, you'll probably see a significant difference. The interesting thing is that if there is a human face in the picture, we tend to center everything around the colour of the face. If the face is wrong, everything is wrong, if the face is right, then everything is right!
